## 1. Definition

**Ergodicity** (as used in the source, in its intuitive rather than fully technical mathematical sense) is the property that, under certain conditions, very long sample paths generated by the same random process come to resemble each other in their statistical properties — and, as the time horizon considered is extended toward infinity, any event a process is structurally exposed to (however rare per period) approaches certainty of eventually occurring.

## 2. Intuition

- Mechanism: a strategy or population observed over a *finite* window may show a sample path with no occurrence of a rare, damaging event, purely because the window was short relative to the event's frequency. As the observation window lengthens, the properties of that single sample path converge toward the properties of the full underlying distribution (the "Monte Carlo properties") — including whatever rare event the strategy is exposed to.
- What determines the practical size of the effect: the rarer the event a strategy is exposed to, the longer a survived sample path can persist without the event occurring, and the more misleadingly "safe" the strategy can appear over any fixed, finite observation window — right up until the horizon is long enough for the event to occur.
- Contrast with treating a survived sample as representative: because of ergodicity, a strategy/trader that has "survived" for N years without encountering its tail risk should not be read as evidence the tail risk does not apply to it — only that N years have not yet been long enough for a low-probability event to occur.

## 3. Mathematical perspective (if applicable)

_(The source does not provide a formal mathematical derivation; it states the property qualitatively — long sample paths converge toward the properties of the process's full distribution, and rare events a process is exposed to occur with certainty as the time horizon is extended to infinity. A full technical treatment of ergodicity, e.g. time-average vs. ensemble-average equivalence conditions, is outside what this vault extracts from this source.)_

## 4. When it matters

- Interpreting any track record (fund, trader, strategy) that has avoided a known tail risk for a period of time: ergodicity is the reason "no failure yet" is weak evidence of "no exposure to failure."
- Evaluating survivorship-selected populations (e.g. today's list of successful hedge funds): the survivors are, mechanically, the sample paths that have not yet encountered their rare event, not evidence that the rare event does not apply to the broader population they were drawn from.
- Risk management for strategies with rare, large downside exposure (short volatility, short tail-risk positions): the longer such a strategy runs without incident, the more its exposure to the eventual rare event should be treated as unchanged, not diminished.

## 6. Related Concepts

- [[C - Survivorship Bias]] — ergodicity is the mechanism this source uses to explain *why* survivorship bias occurs: survivors are simply the sample paths for which the rare, damaging event has not yet happened, not a population that is structurally immune to it.
- [[C - Alternative Histories]] — ergodicity describes how the passage of time converts a merely-possible alternative history into a near-certain eventual outcome.
- [[C - Rare Event Risk (Fat-Tail Mispricing)]] — ergodicity is part of the argument for why rare-event risk is easy to underprice: observers extrapolate from a rare-event-free sample path without recognizing that the sample path's length, not the absence of exposure, explains the absence of the event so far.

## 7. Pitfalls

- Ergodicity is invoked in the source in its intuitive, narrative sense ("long enough and the rare event will happen"), not as a rigorous mathematical proof for any specific process — applying it to a specific strategy still requires estimating the actual frequency/magnitude of the relevant rare event, which the source does not provide a method for.
- The concept does not imply *when* the rare event will occur, only that its probability of occurring approaches 1 as the horizon lengthens — it should not be used to time an exit, only to avoid treating an unrealized-so-far rare event as non-existent.

## 8. Minimal Example

- Of a large initial cohort of speculators, some small fraction will show N consecutive profitable years by chance alone; the source argues that by ergodicity, this "surviving" fraction is expected to fare no better than the initial cohort's failures in any subsequent period — their apparent outperformance is an artifact of the fixed observation window, not of skill that will persist as the window is extended. Source: [[Fooled by Randomness]], Chapters 6 and 9.
